column2: Act Thirteen
The Bloodline Covenant
Blood Contract

Each of you has a human side and a dragon side. In your veins flow many contradictions at once: white and black, good and evil, love and hate, peace and slaughter. We are neither wholly good nor wholly evil. We possess the power to kill, but must not desire to kill. Remember that we stand with humanity. Only those whose human goodness overcomes the evil of dragons are our companions. Anyone who cannot restrain that evil, who lets a hunger for power consume their soul, becomes our enemy.
Lu Mingfei opened his eyes a crack. Warm sunlight fell over him.

He woke with a hangover, reeking of alcohol and naked beneath a sheet. After a few breaths of fresh air, his head cleared a little. He patted the edge of the bed. “Senior, what time is it? You forgot to close the curtains again, didn’t you?”
“With the sun that bright, it must be about noon. Get up and have lunch!” Fingel called from the upper bunk.
The wooden bunk bed began to creak and sway. Apparently Fingel was getting up and preparing to climb down.
“Aaaaaaah!” Fingel suddenly shrieked.
“What are you crowing for? Think you’re a rooster? Even if you were, it’s not morning anymore.” Lu Mingfei pushed himself upright and stretched. “Aaaaaaah!”
“You sound like a hen yourself, and you’re criticizing me...” Fingel muttered. Lu Mingfei, however, could no longer speak.
Their bunk bed stood amid a pile of ruins. One leg had broken off, and a chunk of concrete had taken its place, somehow keeping the bed balanced.

A great Red Cross flag stood in the middle of the rubble, with dozens of white tents pitched beside it. Inside, doctors examined injured students. Occasionally a blood-pressure cuff burst: some hybrids had blood pressure far above that of ordinary humans. Otherwise, all was calm. At the edge of the ruins, cooks had lined up food carts and begun serving breakfast. The smell of Munich white sausages and scallion bread drifted on the breeze. Long lines stretched in front of both the medical station and the breakfast stand, with their bed caught squarely between them.
“Good morning.” Someone from one of the lines came over and shook Lu Mingfei’s hand: Kiran, president of the previous freshmen’s association.
“Hey! Awake?” Lancelot, vice president of the Lionheart Society, waved from a distance.
“We all thought you’d sleep till noon!” Xia Mi stood in front of the bed, smiling, with a cup of milk and cereal in her hands.
“You drink table wine like this? Don’t you find it astringent?” Caesar picked up the bottle by the bed, glanced at its label, and shook his head with disdain.
“Can you really remain so calm in the face of a disaster? I’d like to invite you to take some neurological tests...” Psychology instructor Masashi Toyama looked serious.

Lu Mingfei and Fingel could only pull the sheets tighter around themselves and wave expressionlessly, conveying such complicated sentiments as “I’m fine,” “Don’t worry about us,” and “Please get lost.”

The two brothers had merely shared a drink, discussed life, and talked about their dreams. They hadn’t done anything shameful! How had the world turned upside down while they slept? What was there to stare at? Hadn’t anyone seen a naked man before? Sleeping soundly was a good thing. They were just jealous, weren’t they?

“There was an incident in the Ice Cellar last night. The cause hasn’t been determined. The college announcement said it might have been an earthquake.” Chu Zihang approached the bed. “Several people were injured. No one died.”
Lu Mingfei and Fingel scratched their heads, wearing expressions that said, “Oh, so that’s what happened. What a relief.”
Chu Zihang turned to leave.
“Hey, wait...” Lu Mingfei and Fingel called together.
“What do you need?” Chu Zihang looked back.
“Could... you find me some clothes?” Lu Mingfei asked awkwardly.
“Could... you get me some orange juice and grilled white sausage?” Fingel asked sheepishly. “I’m not wearing anything, so I can’t really get out of bed...”
After several seconds of silence, Lu Mingfei grabbed the wine bottle by the bed and threw it at the upper bunk. “Hey! Have some dignity! Eating is not the priority!”
“There’s no such thing as dignity when you’re hungry!” Fingel declared.

Chu Zihang couldn’t be bothered listening to the pair argue. He looked toward Valhalla. The enormous rooster statue had crashed down and destroyed the mouth of the Foundation Well. Around it, a violent explosion had scorched a black circle dozens of meters across. If that could be explained as an earthquake, Cassell College’s supposed elites had learned nothing. Whoever issued the announcement was obviously lying through their teeth. But with the principal on sick leave and the vice principal in charge, honest college announcements were rare.

The principal’s elevator sank into the sea. The water was not its familiar blue, but a murky red. Dead hammerhead sharks, sea turtles, and bluefin tuna floated beyond the glass, all severed cleanly in two, as though a single sweep of an immensely long blade had cut through them. Their organs spilled from their bodies, digestive tracts drifting through the water like alien sea snakes. It was a vision of hell.
“My fish tank!” Anjou rasped, the corner of his eye twitching.

“I told you, you must stay calm and take things as they come. Suppose someone burned your house down. What good would it do to wander through the ruins screaming, ‘My television!’ or ‘My paintings!’? You’d only make yourself miserable. Look for things you can still use. Those are the surprises. Perhaps you’d find seashells you collected as a child with the little girl next door. Then you’d smile with delight...” The vice principal patted his old friend’s shoulder.
“Don’t drag my intelligence down to your level! Lunatics make everyone else insane and then defeat them with experience in their own field,” Anjou growled.
“Easy, easy. There’s worse...” the vice principal said gently.
The elevator followed its cable into a vast cavern.
“My garden...” Anjou nearly moaned.

Precious trees lay toppled in swaths; those still standing burned fiercely. The shrubs and velvety grass had fared even worse, churned completely to pieces. Black marks crisscrossed the ground, cutting deep into the soil, each broad and nearly a hundred meters long, as though a blazing giant plow had torn through it.
“Think of it as clearing land by fire,” the vice principal said. “You’re lucky you came now. When I arrived this morning, the smoke was so thick I needed a gas mask.”
“My pyramid!” Anjou’s bloodshot eyes nearly bulged from their sockets.

The pyramid of black conglomerate had stood for thousands of years in the American jungle; rain had worn only its surface and corners, proof of its strength. Now an enormous crack split its upper level, exposing the sandstone core. Whatever had struck it was difficult to imagine, but the force had brought down nearly half the structure. Black stones lay scattered around it, and putting them back together would be difficult.

The elevator entered a long, dark tunnel. Beyond it lay the Well of Oblivion. Anjou sat upright, fists clenched so tightly his knuckles cracked. He dared not imagine the devastation there. The intruders’ target had surely been the Well, where every artifact represented vast expense and effort, including the dragonbone over which he had openly clashed with the Board of Trustees.
Everything was ruined. He had merely gone to sleep and woken up.

The elevator doors opened, and a tide of noise poured in. Anjou stared. Someone who knew would say they had come to inspect ruins; anyone else might have thought they were entering an avant-garde band’s recording studio.

The vice principal switched on the lights. There was no band, but a raucous party. Alchemical music boxes played with enthusiasm; Persian-style brass boxes periodically spat flames; a silver-plated skull gaped at Anjou in laughter, its intact teeth clacking together. Without the alchemical domain, these objects containing living spirits had come to life, like little demons escaped from the depths of hell.

In the foulest of moods, Anjou kicked the silver-plated skull away. The kick showed the benefit of more than a decade’s practice: at Cambridge he had been one of the soccer team’s principal defenders.
The vice principal cried out and dived after it. Despite his belly, he caught the skull in midair with the difficult maneuver of a rugby player.
“Don’t take it out on the collection.” The vice principal carefully set the skull aside. “Come and see. There’s a surprise.”

He led Anjou onto the central metal altar, the most severely damaged area. The hard bronze surface had cracked all over; slag that had melted and cooled again littered the floor. A weapon, probably the same one that had sliced the sharks and split the pyramid, had scored countless cuts across it. The altar felt as though it might crumble to powder at any moment.

The vice principal whisked away a black cover like a magician, beaming. “Well? Happy? Surprised? Your fish are dead, your flowers are dead, and half your pyramid has collapsed... but your precious dragonbone is still here!”
The bronze-colored dragonbone stood quietly, intact. The cross-shaped skeleton had the sacred air of a martyr—except that someone had stuck a yellow note in the middle of its forehead.

Anjou was stunned. Before coming down, he had prepared himself to find the dragonbone stolen. Hybrids around the world coveted this relic. A religious thief who slipped into a cathedral and found the Spear of Longinus, the weapon that pierced Jesus, would have no reason not to take it, even if it had not been the original target. Besides, who would risk so much and go to such trouble to enter the Well of Oblivion for anything else? Had the intruder suddenly repented on the verge of success?
The vice principal peeled off the note and handed it to Anjou. “Someone left us a message.”
In lazy, untidy handwriting, it read: “I suggest your college improve its security. Next time someone sneaks in to steal it, I might not happen to be around.” It was unsigned.
“Someone helped you save your collection,” the vice principal said, patting Anjou’s shoulder. “That’s good news and bad news.”
“What do you mean?”

The vice principal pointed to the pool surrounding the altar, now completely dry. “This was the world’s second-largest alchemical domain powered by a mercury solution. I put at least twelve hundred tons of it in there, but some tremendous heat seems to have vaporized it all.”
Anjou stared. “I thought ours was the largest.”

“The largest has yet to be excavated: the tomb of Qin Shi Huang, China’s first emperor. Historical accounts say he had a map of all China carved in his burial chamber, with mercury flowing through it as water—even mercury rain. In ancient Chinese alchemy, that represents perpetual circulation. Historians think it exaggerated, but anyone who studies alchemical domains knows it was an enormous one, powered by mercury. It was so powerful that opponents of his tyranny never dug it up.” The vice principal sighed. “To destroy my domain in an instant would take power approaching that of a first-generation dragon. One of the intruders was undoubtedly a first-generation dragon, yet someone stopped him. That means there was another being of comparable power... though perhaps ‘person’ is hardly the word.” He raised his eyebrows. “Few hybrids can approach a first-generation dragon. Given the damage to the Ice Cellar, two dragons may have fought here last night.”

“Dragons have awakened—more than one—and their power approaches that of first-generation dragons. Even the one who helped us may be an enemy rather than a friend. Is that right?” Anjou’s voice was low.
“Wrong. By your reasoning, all dragons are our enemies.”
Anjou nodded slowly.

“Don’t dwell on it. I’ll move the dragonbone to a new storage facility. Our immediate problem is still the investigation team. They announced this morning that, despite the incident, the hearing will proceed as scheduled. They really can’t wait to bring you down, old friend,” the vice principal said.
Zhao Menghua sat in the darkness, dazed, as the subway train rumbled onward.

In the end, he had boarded the rust-streaked train because he had nowhere else to go. He had sobbed and screamed on the platform, hidden trembling behind a pillar—done everything a desperate person might do. No one paid him any attention. Not even a monster came out to frighten him. Finally, lying breathless on the platform, he remembered some philosopher saying that death was terrible not because of pain but because of eternal loneliness.

The train was empty too, but its rumbling movement felt better than the platform. Remarkably, it passed stations where lights shone and passengers waited. Yet the train sped through without slowing, and the passengers remained calm, as if they could not see it. Zhao Menghua pressed against the window and shouted, but outside, people kept reading, listening to music, or staring into space. One little brat even struck an Ultraman pose at him—though he was probably admiring his reflection in the glass doors.
The child belonged to 2010, and Zhao Menghua belonged to 1992. A chasm of time separated them.
Feeling cold, Zhao Menghua curled up and shoved his hands into his pockets. His fingertips touched something.
His phone!
Only then did he remember he had brought it. He had been on his way to Zhongguancun to get it repaired!

He pulled it out and looked. Darkness swam before his eyes. He had forgotten to charge it the night before; the battery had run flat and the phone had shut itself off. A large-screen smartphone lasted only a day and needed charging every night.

Zhao Menghua slumped in his seat. A figure in white crossed his mind—not a ghost, but Chen Wenwen. He had stopped charging his phone every night because they had broken up. When they were together, he charged it nightly because Chen Wenwen was sensitive and wanted him to keep it on at all times so she could always reach him. Every night before bed she sent a message: “Good night. Remember to charge your phone.”

When you break up with someone, you say goodbye to everything connected with her. You stop eating at her favorite restaurant and close the blog you shared. A scene in a movie once made her cry for no apparent reason and rub against your shoulder; afterward, whenever you see it, you instinctively turn away and draw in your shoulder.
And of course you no longer wait for her little anxious messages: “Where are you?” “I had a dream.” “Is it the start of winter today? It’s getting dark so early... What are you doing?”

None of that is much, really. Prettier girls will take you to better restaurants. You move on to Weibo and meet selfie experts who post low-cut glamour shots every day. There will always be new midnight movies for every kind of sentimental girl to wash your shirt with tears. Your life will still be full.
But when you are trapped in an enclosed space with only a phone to call for help, you discover that, like an idiot, you also said goodbye to charging it every night!
It had taken her so long to teach you that habit...
Maybe there was still a little charge? Zhao Menghua thought. After a phone shut down, the battery always recovered a little. Turn it on again, and it might last a few minutes.

A few minutes would be enough! With trembling hands, he pressed the power button. The screen lit up. The smartphone took so long to start that his heart pounded. He stared at it, terrified the battery would suddenly die. If a pedal-powered generator had appeared before him, he would gladly have traded his expensive Rolex for it!
It started! But there was no signal...

Zhao Menghua was frantic. He remembered now: Beijing’s subway tunnels had no mobile transmitters. There was a signal only at stations. He pressed his face to the window and stared ahead. Finally, a glow appeared. The next station was coming up. Two bars suddenly appeared on his phone!
There really was a signal! But the train would pass without slowing, leaving him barely a dozen seconds. He had to dial quickly. The battery would last only this one station.

But his phone was broken: he couldn’t open his contacts. Zhao Menghua froze, his mind blank. He didn’t remember his parents’ numbers, his roommates’ numbers, or Liu Miaomiao’s. Young Master Zhao never bothered with such details. The only number he remembered was 114, directory assistance. But if he called and said, Hello, I’m trapped on a pitch-black subway train, I’m so scared, can you rescue me? the operator would probably reply politely, Certainly. I’ll put you through to a psychiatric hospital.
He had only seconds. He had to call someone who would believe him—believe him unconditionally!

There was another number, though its owner no longer appeared in his contacts. He had deleted her. He remembered her number because she had once made him recite it over and over. Until he learned it, he was not allowed to keep strolling beneath the streetlights with his arm around her waist. That way, she said, whether he lost his phone or found himself trekking through wilderness with no signal, he could always find her with that number.

She had said sentimental, literary things like, “Look, eleven digits are all it takes to find someone. You can find me for the rest of your life, because I won’t change my number or switch my phone off.” And she had used the promise of more strolling with his arm around her waist to make him memorize those jumbled digits.
Alone in the empty darkness, Zhao Menghua murmured, “138...” The patternless numbers tumbled from his lips one by one, as if his lips and tongue remembered them rather than his brain.
The lips and tongue that had once kissed a girl.
The call connected. No one spoke. There was only faint breathing.
“Wenwen, save me...” Tears streamed down Zhao Menghua’s face. His breath was like the feeble white mist of someone freezing to death in the depths of a winter night.
Valhalla conference hall.

Outside, the rooster statue still stood upside down in the Foundation Well, its rear pointing skyward like a roast chicken on a platter. The rubble had not yet been cleared, but the hearing began on schedule. It was the biggest event at the college: for the first time in a century, the principal faced impeachment. Chu Zihang was on trial, but everyone knew he was Anjou’s proxy.

Chu Zihang stood inside the square wooden railing at the center of the hall, expressionless, nodding to the jury. Department heads and tenured professors, all dressed in black, were taking their seats at the front. They looked old enough to have been dug out of graves. Their faces were solemn, but their manners varied: some smoked pipes, some chewed chunks of celery, and one blew bubble-gum bubbles with brightly shining eyes.
“They look like a bunch of idiots,” Fingel whispered behind the vice principal. “Not half as dashing as you and the principal, boss!”

“But they are the college’s foundations. The Executive, Information, and Equipment Departments all depend on their research. Without them, there would be no Cassell College.” The vice principal sighed. “The Board of Trustees is ruthless, dragging these old researchers out to rule on college affairs. They’re so easy to fool.”
“If the other side can fool them, so can we.”
“That’s my student! How did Guderian ever become your adviser? You should be studying the highest art of shamelessness with me!” the vice principal said admiringly.

Opposite them sat the entire investigation team, Andrew at its head and Parsi immediately beside him. Andrew glared at his enemies, eyes blazing. He had sworn to avenge their humiliation of him; his plump, pale face twitched.
“Andrew, my boy, are you all right? Your face is twitching,” the vice principal called across the room. “Not ill, are you?”
The old bastard had made a fool of Andrew again. Unable to think of a reply, he turned his head sharply away.
“Trying to play with me,” the vice principal snorted. “Youngsters.”
“How old are you, Vice Principal?” Fingel asked.
“Twenty-five.”
Fingel blinked. He vaguely knew the vice principal belonged to the same generation as Anjou, who was at least a hundred and thirty.
“The golden age that will never leave me. Forever twenty-five!” Looking perfectly serious, the vice principal waved to Manstein in the audience. “Hello, son!”
Like Andrew, Manstein turned his head away. He did not want to acknowledge his idiot father in public.

The selected student representatives were taking their seats. The Lionheart Society had secured half the places. All its members wore crimson uniforms with white neck scarves, as orderly as an army. The Student Council held the other half. Never willing to match the Lionheart Society, they had chosen black uniforms. Caesar’s prized troupe of girls in white lace now appeared in long black lace dresses, apparently ready to bury their rivals. The two sides occupied the left and right halves of the hall.

Student Council president Caesar Gattuso had plainly come to enjoy the spectacle. Wearing headphones, he listened happily to music. The campus paparazzi, meanwhile, noticed that neither society leader’s woman had appeared: Nono and Susie were both absent.

There was still someone whose beauty commanded the room. Xia Mi, the strongest candidate for campus beauty among the freshmen, led a group of lovestruck boys from the freshmen’s association to the Lionheart side. She held a bouquet of unopened fragrant lilies; anyone could guess its intended recipient with their eyes closed. Of course, if things turned ugly, no one could guarantee she wouldn’t beat Andrew with it...

The last heavyweight to arrive was Lu Mingfei, the college’s only S-rank student. Head lowered, he sat in a corner on the Lionheart side. His discretion was understandable: photographs of him and News Department head Fingel eating grilled sausages wrapped in white sheets had recently reached alumni inboxes around the world. He seemed to have some loyalty, choosing not to sit with the Student Council even though Caesar was his boss. Everyone knew, however, how much Chu Zihang had looked after him on their mission in China.
“Caesar’s girls are formidable opponents!” The vice principal frowned.
“How so?” Fingel asked.

“A hearing is like a soccer match. We’re playing against the investigation team. It isn’t just about footwork; the cheerleading lineups matter too. I think their side has more beautiful girls!” The vice principal looked troubled.
Fingel nodded. “But we have Xia Mi. She’s worth ten of theirs!”
“Yes, she’s the only girl who gives me comfort... I’m really looking forward to watching her swimming test.” The vice principal nodded slightly.
King Solomon tapped his gavel. The hall fell silent.

“I declare this hearing open,” King Solomon said solemnly. “The Board of Trustees’ investigation team and the college administration disagree over the bloodline of A-rank student Chu Zihang. We must therefore hold this hearing to allow an open discussion. In the documents submitted beforehand, the investigation team strongly condemned the administration’s negligence. The administration described that condemnation as...” He lowered his eyes to read. “‘Nonsense like a frog looking up at the sky from a well!’ I quote the vice principal verbatim. Unfortunately, I do not fully understand the sentence.”

“A frog at the bottom of a well,” the vice principal corrected. “A Chinese idiom. A frog, toad, or similar creature sits at the bottom of a well, looks up, and says, Ah, the sky is only that big? It’s smaller than my well! By extension, it describes certain narrow-minded, conceited people holding forth about things they know nothing about.”
“A wonderfully vivid rhetorical device,” King Solomon observed. He adored rhetoric.
Andrew’s fury could have blown the roof off Valhalla. Snickers rose from the Lionheart side of the audience.
“Now, let both parties present their evidence. You may argue, but the final judgment rests with us.” King Solomon brought down the gavel again.

Like a boxer at the opening bell, Andrew sprang up. “The Board of Trustees has ample evidence to support its concerns about the administration! Over the past decade, laxity has spread throughout the campus. The committees have failed to supervise and guide students effectively. The academic workload is too light; the Freedom Day event is irresponsible; bloodline rankings are assigned arbitrarily. Worse still, the Executive Department has become an organization of violence!” He slammed a stack of papers onto the table.

“It hasn’t become anything. The Board simply doesn’t understand our history. The Executive Department has always been an organization of violence!” its head retorted from the audience, his voice hoarse and cold.

The Executive Department’s elites applauded thunderously. Schneider was telling the truth. They were not ashamed of being violent; their only regret was that they were less violent than the Equipment Department.
“Order!” King Solomon tapped his gavel. “Presenting the documents matters more than quarreling!”
“Very well!” Andrew said loudly. “The first document the Board wishes to disclose is Chu Zihang’s Executive Department file!” Another document hit the table.

“Being loud doesn’t make you right,” the vice principal said calmly. “Chu Zihang? A fine boy, excellent in both character and scholarship! Outstanding grades, named an all-around model student two years running—no, I mean awarded the Principal’s Scholarship. And unusually kindhearted. All our students know he often helps old ladies across the street.”
Laughter swept the audience.

“Really? Then explain the collapse of the Cape Town baseball stadium! Sovereign Flame, a high-risk Yanling, used in front of tens of thousands! Yet none of it was mentioned in the mission report. What are you hiding?” Andrew demanded.
“It was mentioned in the report.” The vice principal snapped his fingers. “Read it!”

Fingel unfolded a document. “Note: a minor disturbance occurred during the operation, resulting in several minor injuries and fires. The Cape Town fire service promptly extinguished the flames, which did not spread. Chu Zihang received a demerit and forfeited one month’s scholarship.”
“See? Very strict! We supervise our students very strictly! It’s all clearly stated!” the vice principal declared.

“A minor disturbance? Tens of thousands watched the Cape Town baseball stadium collapse! Hundreds suffered burns!” Andrew shouted. “Cape Town television broadcast this to millions. The footage has been submitted to the jury. How do you explain that?”
“Speaking of which... I happened to watch a Cape Town television special yesterday, precisely about that incident.” The vice principal snapped his fingers again. “Play the video!”

A television program appeared on the large screen, the station’s logo in the upper right. A reporter was interviewing an elderly Black man with an earnest expression, who showed the reporter a burn scar on his arm.
“What can you recall about the stadium incident, which has yet to receive a satisfactory explanation?” the reporter asked.
“I saw the man responsible!” The elderly man nodded firmly.
“Can you describe his appearance?”

“Red and blue clothes. A tight suit and a cape. He looked like a lunatic. Fire came out of his eyes, and the clothes burned right off any woman he looked at!” The elderly man’s expression said he had seen it clearly, beyond any doubt.
The shot changed to a young man in hip-hop clothes. “Definitely an American. Square face.”
“A tight suit, lots of muscles. Very handsome,” said a shy girl.
“I saw him lift a Hummer and throw it. I don’t know who he was fighting,” said a security guard who had been there.
The camera returned to the reporter. “After months of investigating the stadium’s collapse, we have unexpectedly discovered that eyewitness descriptions all point to a familiar figure...”
The image froze. A full-screen portrait of a certain famous alien appeared: blue tights, red underwear on the outside, a red cape, and that coquettish little curl on his forehead...
Andrew’s eyes nearly popped from their sockets. “You mean... Superman did it?”
The vice principal shrugged. “I didn’t say anything. Cape Town television did.”
Andrew hammered both fists on the table. “Enough! I’ve put up with you long enough! Don’t treat me like a fool! If you’re going to deceive me, at least invent something believable!”
“We aren’t deceiving you.” The vice principal shook his head helplessly. “I’m merely showing you television. The world is so lovely, yet you’re so irritable.”
“What about Stockholm? Chu Zihang hanged a criminal from the city hall!”
“A serial killer—and a death servitor. Hanging him was perfectly normal. A fitting end.” The vice principal looked unconcerned.

“But during the operation Chu Zihang was clearly on the verge of losing control! He showed dangerous homicidal tendencies, caused by his bloodline! That was erased from the report!” Andrew sneered. “How do you explain it?”
“Oh, about that. Let’s look at some witnesses the police recently found,” the vice principal said.
The screen changed. “Definitely Spider-Man. Look at the way the man was strung up. That’s his handiwork. I recognize it,” a freckled boy in a backward baseball cap said confidently.
“A figure climbed the city hall very quickly, using both hands and feet, straight up the wall. Whoosh, whoosh.” The witness spoke fluent Mandarin; the subtitles identified him as a Chinese tourist.
“I know you also want to ask about Chicago’s Hancock building.” The vice principal pressed the remote.

“I saw him. He winked at me. Very handsome. Sexy.” A drunken woman sprawled on a barstool with her legs apart, a pose both seductive and indecent. She narrowed her eyes as though flirting with the cameraman. “He drove away in an Audi TT. That’s right, Iron Man. It was him. Everyone knows that face. I think he’d have stayed for a drink if he hadn’t been in a hurry.”

“Repulsor Rays in both hands, a Uni-Beam in his chest. He fired like this and blasted through three floors of walls at once! Believe me, he’s the strongest, because Iron Man can keep upgrading himself! Those superheroes who depend on genes can’t compare. He did it. I saw it myself.” A café employee posed with both hands firing beams. “Afterward? Don’t listen to that stupid woman. Of course he flew away! Do you know anything about Iron Man? He can fly! Why would he need an Audi?”

The vice principal turned gracefully, spread his hands, and smiled. “After watching these reports, my dear colleagues, our great scientists and wise theologians, can we believe Superman, Iron Man, or Spider-Man did these things?” He slammed the table. “Obviously not! Can the public media be admitted as evidence? They’re a pack of paparazzi! They’ll fabricate anything for a sensational story!” He looked deeply grieved. “Why distrust Executive Department reports while believing the media? As vice principal, I have diligently insisted for years that the Executive Department seek truth, conduct itself honorably, and work conscientiously. That is the spirit of our century-old school motto... Oh, sorry. We have no motto.” He cleared his throat. “Friends! Keep your eyes open! We shall never let a villain escape, nor falsely accuse an innocent!”

The investigation team looked as though lightning had struck them. They had guessed these people’s standards were low; they hadn’t guessed they had none at all. Cassell College’s most shameless paparazzi were smearing the entire world’s media as paparazzi to discredit its evidence.

After a brief silence, Fingel led every Lionheart representative to their feet in applause. Schneider led the attending professors in another standing ovation. Only Caesar and the Student Council representatives remained seated. The jurors exchanged glances. Many of these elderly scientists and theologians had not left campus for years and knew little of developments outside. Some had read Superman or Spider-Man comics, and some were fans. But comic-book heroes obviously could not appear in reality. It followed, just as the vice principal had said, that the media had degenerated over recent decades and could no longer be trusted. The investigation team’s evidence would therefore have difficulty passing muster.
The tenured professors all nodded.
The heavy conference-hall doors creaked open, admitting a shaft of sunlight into the gloom.

Sitting beside the door, Lu Mingfei turned and saw a crimson uniform skirt, dark-red hair tied with a white silk ribbon, high-heeled crimson suede boots, and silver four-leaf-clover earrings gleaming beside her face.

For a moment he was back more than a year earlier, when his small world had extended no farther than a city in southern China. This little red-haired witch had opened a door in exactly the same way. Light had poured in, and she had stood within it, beautiful brows and eyes full of disdain. An angel descending, sword in hand. She had brutally torn an opening in his world; otherwise he would never have been here at a meeting with reptilian hybrids.
He smiled dazedly.
“Move over. Make room.” Nono kicked him.

A stir ran through the audience. The Student Council president’s girlfriend had arrived late, wearing the Lionheart Society’s crimson uniform—and sat down on the Lionheart side! Caesar seemed not to notice her arrival. He did not turn, continuing to listen intently through his noise-canceling headphones.
“What are you doing here?” Lu Mingfei murmured.

After that long, hot summer, he and Nono had lost contact like a kite with a broken string. She hadn’t even sent him a birthday message, though she had promised not to forget. Then he learned Caesar had applied for permission to become engaged to her. Was the engagement why? The bride-to-be was busy preparing her dress and everything else; he scarcely saw her on campus anymore.

He didn’t really want to see her either. He admitted he was envious, jealous, resentful, and a little angry with her. She had been inexplicably loyal to him, always offering a glimmer of hope, yet could vanish in an instant because she had never promised anything. Why give him hope at all? Hadn’t the Little Match Girl died because she had too much hope? Light one match: wow, a turkey! Another: wow, a cake! Another: wow, Mom! None of those hopes could come true, so the girl died.
If the Little Match Girl had spent her time finding somewhere warm to hide instead of hoping, she might have survived that freezing winter night.
Hope that you must eventually lose was poison.
He had decided to avoid Nono until he could firmly establish “Caesar’s fiancée” as her identity in his mind. Then he would see her and wish them a long, happy marriage.
But he had failed to avoid her. Seeing her, his heart trembled, and all he could manage was that disconnected question.
“What are you doing here... Didn’t you already leave?”
“Why can’t I come?” Nono raised an eyebrow.
“There are sides here. Caesar’s over there,” Lu Mingfei said quietly.
“I know.” Nono pointed to the Student Council delegation, all dressed in black. “I prefer red.”
Lu Mingfei froze. He knew she liked red—so much that she chose strawberry sauce on her ice cream because it matched her hair. But could hair color determine which side you took?
“Victory is ours!” The vice principal beamed. “Now our beauties surpass theirs in both quantity and quality!”
“But we can’t be sure those old men judge the result by the cheerleaders,” Fingel said.

“What the old men think hardly matters. They’ve lost their eye for beautiful women. The point is to undermine Andrew’s morale! Wouldn’t a creepy middle-aged man hate seeing a more magnificent cheerleading squad on the other side?” The vice principal twisted his hips, made faces at Andrew across the room, and performed Michael Jackson’s signature crotch grab. Even Fingel thought the old man’s provocation vulgar.

“Order! Ladies and gentlemen, please curtail unnecessary disputes. This hearing concerns whether the administration made a serious error in bloodline assessment and admitted a dangerous bloodline to campus,” King Solomon said sternly. “This is among our greatest taboos. In ancient times, we established ironclad rules under the Abraham Bloodline Covenant to purge impure bloodlines from our midst. Those rules remain in force. On the day you enrolled, you signed your agreement to obey them. We are all therefore bound by them...”
Only now did Lu Mingfei understand the draconian agreement he had signed on enrollment.

“Each of you has a human side and a dragon side. In your veins flow many contradictions at once: white and black, good and evil, love and hate, peace and slaughter. We are neither wholly good nor wholly evil. We possess the power to kill, but must not desire to kill. Remember that we stand with humanity. Only those whose human goodness overcomes the evil of dragons are our companions. Anyone who cannot restrain that evil, who lets a hunger for power consume their soul, becomes our enemy.” King Solomon closed the heavy code, the Abraham Bloodline Covenant. “At that moment our covenant ends, and our blades will turn upon the one who has fallen into the abyss.”
Everyone placed a hand over the left side of their chest in respect for the sacred code.
“Bold of you, Ricardo. A Student Council member sitting on Chu Zihang’s side? Aren’t you afraid Caesar will beat you up?” Nono whispered.
“Who isn’t afraid of getting beaten up by the boss? But you have to be loyal. Chu Zihang’s been good to me.” Lu Mingfei ducked his head. “And this could cost him his life.”
“Nonsense! That can’t be your reason. Your reason should be that you take the same side as your big sis!” Nono glared. “Remember, you’re my little brother, not Caesar’s!”

Lu Mingfei stared at her, searching her beautiful, imperious face for a hint of something. There was nothing. She was simply beautiful and imperious, her brows lively. Her faint fragrance reached him, and he suddenly realized he was sitting right beside her. God alone knew why she had felt so far away until then.
“Brother, wake up to the situation!” a little voice clamored in his head. “Nono’s on your side. Caesar’s on the other side. Right now she’s closer to you than to Caesar!”

“Honorable investigators, the debate thus far suggests the media are not a reliable source. Questioning the bloodline of one of our own is a serious matter. We require stronger examples.” King Solomon turned to Andrew.
“Then I request permission to question some of those involved.” Andrew stood and approached the audience.
He stopped beside Lu Mingfei. “Lu Mingfei, you and Chu Zihang carried out a mission together in China. What is your opinion of him?”
Lu Mingfei froze. He had not expected this. Only when Nono dug her heel into his foot did he leap up as though his backside were spring-loaded.
“Very... very loyal,” he stammered.

The utterly irrelevant answer deflated half of Andrew’s aggression, just as his forceful arrival at Cassell College had been met with the vice principal’s absurd banquet. He had thought a surprise attack on this student might work. But the boy was evidently worthy of his S-rank and had absorbed the college’s boundless shamelessness. He could not be underestimated.

Andrew decided on a frontal assault and placed a document before Lu Mingfei. “This is the mission report you signed. According to it, everything went smoothly and ended perfectly. In fact, Chu Zihang departed entirely from the plan and acted alone, didn’t he? You have no idea what he did without a third person present, do you?”

“Absolutely not! We’re honest people! We stand by our word! Chu Zihang followed orders and observed discipline!” Lu Mingfei committed himself. He had little choice: Nono had stealthily pinched his calf. It was an open threat.

“Really? Are you qualified to say that?” Sneering, Andrew placed another document before him. “While dozens were injured and the entire twenty-first floor of the Runde Building was destroyed, you were dining with a girl at the luxurious Aspasia restaurant! You took no part in the operation, did you? Here is your dinner receipt—paid, remarkably, by our Gattuso family. I can’t help admiring your influence, Mr. Lu. Then, having wiped your mouth after dinner, you wrote this utterly irresponsible report saying everything went smoothly?”
“What’s wrong with eating with a classmate? She’d had a breakup and needed comfort...” Lu Mingfei stammered.

Sweat broke out on his forehead. He did not know how to handle this. Chu Zihang had indeed written the report for him; he had signed without reading it and been dragged into the mess. Worse, he didn’t even know what had happened at the Runde Building that night. He had no way to defend Chu Zihang.

“Ladies and gentlemen, the vice principal said media evidence is unreliable. Should we now also question our own internal reports? These apparently straightforward documents are tools used to conceal the truth: Chu Zihang’s lack of control, dangerous personal style, and extreme methods on every operation. Above all, they conceal the bloodline problem behind it...” Andrew’s voice rose abruptly, commanding the hall.
“All right, all right, I admit it.” Lu Mingfei’s voice was louder still.
The hall fell silent. Everyone looked at Lu Mingfei.

Lu Mingfei cleared his throat. “All right. I formally admit I tampered with the report. I altered the operational plan, and what happened differed from the report. The truth is, I had dinner plans with a classmate that evening, so I sent Chu Zihang to retrieve the documents alone. I revised the plan in a hurry, which led to the destruction of the Runde Building’s twenty-first floor. But I was on the phone with Chu Zihang throughout and confirmed everything was under control. I admit I falsified the report, but that has nothing to do with Chu Zihang.”
“Absurd! You have no field experience. How could you devise a new plan? You couldn’t possibly control Chu Zihang!” Andrew raged.
“But I was the commissioner.” Lu Mingfei scratched his temple. “A higher rank carries weight.”

He rolled his eyes and stared at Andrew. Consider it repayment to Chu Zihang. Besides... Nono was still twisting his calf! They were on the same side now. He could be a coward another time, but not now.

He turned to Nono to see whether his words had landed. She looked at him too, baring her teeth in a silent grin. Such a wicked grin, yet it made him feel as though he were floating. Suddenly he understood why that idiot King You of Zhou had lit the warning beacons to toy with his lords. Damn it, if it made the girl you liked smile, even overthrowing the Board of Trustees wasn’t beyond Lu Mingfei.
He was the sort of person who could go mad for some peculiar reason!
“You mean the discrepancies in the report were entirely your responsibility?” King Solomon asked.
“Absolutely! I led that operation. Naturally I’m responsible.”
“Understand that your record is currently clean. If you maintain this position, you will receive a serious demerit.”
“Will my rank go down?”
“That requires discussion, but it is possible. You are our only S-rank student. You could lose that distinction.”
“Oh, it’s only my rank? I thought you were stealing my eggs.” Lu Mingfei settled firmly into his seat.

After several seconds of silence, thunderous applause erupted. The Lionheart students’ excitement peaked. Most did not understand the Chinese joke, but the vice principal was doubled over the table, pounding it, so it must be some devastating satire. They collectively pretended to understand and applauded. Andrew was engulfed by the noise. He hadn’t understood either, but apparently everyone else had and was mocking him through their applause. He had no idea how to respond. Fury and humiliation made him stare so hard his eyes felt ready to split.

(Author’s note: This is a bawdy joke. A village woman takes a basket of eggs to market. Several thugs find her attractive and try to seize and rape her, but she fights bravely with a rolling pin and leaves them battered and bleeding. Astonished, they say they never expected such a fiercely chaste woman: someone like her must not be touched. Only then does she understand. “Oh, is that all? I thought you were stealing my eggs!”)
Nono was pounding the table with laughter too. Lu Mingfei stole a sideways glance at her. Such an arrogant laugh, but he longed to see it. When she laughed, the distance between them seemed smaller.
He was happy. A joke had set the whole room roaring, but all he had wanted was to amuse this girl.

“I will tolerate no more insults.” Andrew strode back to the investigators’ table. “Next I shall present evidence that cannot possibly be dismissed!” He surveyed the room. “Chu Zihang’s blood sample!”
The vice principal froze.
“Haven’t they noticed his blood was replaced?” Fingel whispered.
“I know they lack intelligence, but this degree of stupidity actually worries me...” The vice principal leaned closer. “No samples got out, did they?”
“All destroyed. Not a drop left.”

Carrying a medical freezer box, Parsi walked to the center of the hall and placed a piece of quartz glass on a small table. He opened the box. A transparent evacuated tube stood in dry ice; the blood inside was black as petroleum.

“Our next evidence is an experiment. It is somewhat dangerous, so please keep your distance. As everyone knows, dragon blood strongly attacks human blood. Sometimes it strengthens the human body, as in myths of heroes bathing in dragon blood and becoming invulnerable. Usually, however, dragon blood is deadly poison to humans. The blood of hybrids with high-risk bloodlines has similar properties: uncontrollable, burning blood of evil that reacts violently with human blood.”
The head of Genetic Biology was the first department chair to nod. This was textbook knowledge, though few people obtained fresh dragon blood and human blood for experiments.
Parsi raised the evacuated tube. “I drew this sample directly from Chu Zihang, immediately sealed it, and kept it refrigerated. It has not been opened since. Is that correct, Chu Zihang?”
“Yes,” Chu Zihang said.
“This other sample is pure human blood from a blood bank.” Parsi raised another quartz tube. “Its provenance can be verified. We will now take one drop from each sample and bring them into contact.”

Using a pipette, he placed a drop of each blood sample on the quartz glass. An arched groove in its center guided the drops slowly together. They met but did not mix, like oil and water, merely adhering slightly. Suddenly Parsi darted backward. Brilliant red burst from the glass like flung ink, a flower opening in midair, or a crimson fountain. The reaction was as violent as sodium dropped into water. Fine threads of liquid splashed out, leaving black marks across the tabletop.
Everyone rose in astonishment.
“Damn it! How?” The vice principal stared. That reaction was unique to Chu Zihang’s blood. He and Anjou had performed the experiment themselves.
Central Control Room. Even during the hearing, an Executive Department team remained on duty here, monitoring information worldwide.
A young Executive Department member kept refreshing the Hunter Market website. The college always monitored it, and surveillance had intensified after the previous incident.

Everything looked normal today. The posted jobs seemed unremarkable: mostly illicit trafficking in antiquities, with some requests for exorcisms and ghost hunting, and an invitation to dive in search of Atlantis. Hunters needed strong nerves. Otherwise, spending their days among illegal, irrational, inexplicable things occurring quite calmly on this forum might make them doubt they were still on Earth.
A bold title rose to the top of the forum. It had been posted only minutes earlier, yet already had an astonishing seventy replies—a number reached only by exceptionally hot threads here.
The young man glanced at it and began to tremble. He lacked even the courage to open it. Instinctively he pressed F5. In barely a dozen seconds, the replies passed a hundred.

The website suddenly slowed. Clearly the information was racing through fiber-optic cables around the world. Countless users were opening the thread, overwhelming the server with simultaneous requests.
This terrifying post would be a nuclear explosion throughout the hybrid world.
Parsi returned silently to the table, leaving the experimental bench almost scorched by the blood. Words were no longer needed to establish the sample’s danger. The experiment had been horrifying.

The vice principal’s expression darkened. As an alchemy expert, he knew this experiment could not be faked. That was blood refined by blood amplification, exceptionally unstable. But how had the sample escaped?

The tenured professors gathered and whispered. The experiment had shaken them too. They had to consider the danger: perhaps the silent student Chu Zihang carried blood like aqua regia throughout his body and might turn into a death servitor at any moment.
The students exchanged glances. Inside the wooden railing, Chu Zihang remained expressionless.
“Who can guarantee it came from Chu Zihang?” Xia Mi suddenly stood. “No one saw you draw it, did they? Maybe you just added concentrated nitric acid. Why not draw blood here?”
“Because his blood has been replaced! The body needs a month to regenerate all its blood. Wash it out as you would treat a critically ill patient, and all evidence disappears!” Andrew said loudly.
“If all his blood was like that, wouldn’t contact with normal blood during the transfusion cause an explosion? How could he be sitting here?” Nono stood too.

Moments later, the Lionheart students rallied, applauding thunderously. A combined attack by beautiful girls really was a trump card. If Chu Zihang’s blood reacted violently with fresh blood, how could a transfusion be performed?

The vice principal bared his teeth slightly. He knew the answer. Anjou’s ruthlessness bordered on madness: he had indeed drained every drop of Chu Zihang’s blood before introducing new blood. His body, strengthened by blood amplification, had sustained him through half an hour of life-threatening total blood loss.

“We don’t yet know how they replaced it. But wait! There is more evidence!” Andrew sprang up, slapping the table. “Witness testimony! Ask Chu Zihang’s classmates whether he really is the obedient, disciplined student the administration describes—or a potential tyrannosaur!” He pointed to Caesar. “I ask the tenured professors to hear the testimony of Student Council president Caesar Gattuso, an outstanding A-rank student!”

Silence returned. Everyone knew Caesar would oppose Chu Zihang: they were sworn rivals, the kind who delighted in each other’s misfortune. Besides, eliminating the Lionheart Society would leave the Student Council as the college’s largest organization. Its leader might become the future leader of the Dragon Blood Secret Party.

Caesar removed his noise-canceling headphones, adjusted his collar, and slowly stood. He bowed slightly to the tenured professors, then nodded to both sides like a performer about to sing. “Ladies and gentlemen, I, Caesar Gattuso, swear upon my family name that everything I say here is true. Chu Zihang is our college’s finest student and a good classmate to us all. We are all deeply drawn to his personal charm. He is refined, gentle, learned, and helpful: the graceful embodiment of every virtue...”

As that beautiful baritone flowed, Andrew felt his world collapse. What was happening? Hadn’t he sworn on his family name? How could he still tell such shameless lies? The graceful embodiment of every virtue? Was that Chu Zihang, or Shakyamuni after attaining Buddhahood?
“Caesar cares little for his surname, just as he cares little for the family,” Parsi whispered into his ear.

Once everyone realized Caesar was neither being sarcastic nor preparing a reversal, applause threatened to lift the roof. Caesar began an emotional account of working on a paper with Chu Zihang: helping each other, draping his coat over a classmate asleep at a library desk late at night, sailing across the great lake together and discussing their ambitions to slay dragons... Did they need to sound so devoted? The students went wild. Caesar Gattuso had never shown such a sense of humor. Lionheart and Student Council members stood and exchanged seats, mingling black and crimson.
They were no longer opponents. Before the investigation team, they had become friends.

Lu Mingfei suddenly understood. This was the greatest mockery of the investigators. Everyone in the audience had reached an unspoken agreement long ago. The boundary between black and crimson was merely a trick. The whole college stood united against the Board. Only he hadn’t known. For days he had sat drinking cheap red wine and staring into space. For days he had never left his room. For days everyone had left him behind.
Nono was no longer beside him. Laughing at Caesar’s deadpan jokes, she jumped up and rushed to embrace him. Black and crimson clustered around them.

Lu Mingfei applauded with everyone else. What else could he do? He ought to be happy. Now everyone was on his side. Together they had given the investigators a thorough drubbing. Even the tenured professors would have to consider the entire student body’s opinion, wouldn’t they? His expressionless senior would escape disaster.

Only he was a fool. They had planned it all; only he had been left out. Just like the time, years ago, when he had played a lowercase i... But the person who had rescued him then was now embracing her boyfriend. She too had become one of “them.”

The pressure of the crowd forced him backward, step by step, until he reached a corner and seemed flattened against the wall. No one noticed him. Everyone was celebrating. Only one gaze crossed the crowd and rested silently upon him, unnoticed by Lu Mingfei.
It was Chu Zihang. He had suddenly lifted his bowed head.
The conference-hall doors flew open. The young man from the Executive Department rushed inside.
“No interruptions during the hearing!” King Solomon said loudly.

“Hunter Market... a new bounty!” The young man panted. “A dragon called Fenrisulfr... awakened in Beijing, China... recruiting hunters to kill him... the reward is a hundred million... a hundred million dollars!”

Dead silence. King Solomon stared for a long time, then sank into his chair. This truly was a nuclear bomb—an information bomb. Someone had posted this on a public site like Hunter Market. The secret of dragons, guarded by hybrids for thousands of years, was about to leak. Hybrids were far from the only people on that website.

Chu Zihang suddenly raised his hand, his voice carrying through the hall. “Professors, if the hearing cannot reach a conclusion, I wish to prove myself through action. Under these circumstances, we are bound to send commissioners to China. Lu Mingfei and I have carried out a mission there together before. I request permission to go with him again. My actions will prove my bloodline.”
